BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,,,Mr. Speaker, may I say just a few words with regard to Russia's entry into the league. When the ban was placed upon Russian imports one recalls the statement that accompanied the order in council:

The government is convinced that there is forced labour in the cutting and transport of timber, and the mining of coal, that political prisoners are exploited, that the standard of living is below any level conceived of in Canada, and that, broadly speaking, all employment is in control of the communist government which regulates all conditions of work and seeks to impose its will upon the whole world. This is communism, its creed and its fruits, which we as a country oppose and must refuse to support by interchange of trade.

I am glad that notwithstanding that declaration on the part of the Minister of National Revenue the government of Canada saw fit to sign the invitation to Russia to enter the league. It seems to me that the hon. member for Labelle, in trying to stress one particular point, took an altogether exaggerated position. I wonder if he would say that Europe was Christian in the fractricidal war of 1914 to 1918. I wonder if he would affirm that Hitler's Germany is Christian today. I wonder if he would venture to say that Japan is Christian. During the recent visit I paid to that country I remember seeing the tablets that commemorate the extirpation of Christianity in that country. It is true that after Commodore Perry bombarded Japan the missionaries were allowed to return, but still only a very small percentage of the people of Japan are Christian and I do not
know that anyone can say that that empire is proceeding along Christian lines. I think the hon. member for Labelle was much nearer the mark when he made this statement on May 27, 1931:
But, Mr. Speaker, I would not be a Christian,

I would not be a British subject, and I would not be imbued with the principles of social liberty, if I would not assert at the same time that the economic system under which the United States and' Canada have grown, progressed or retrograded, for the last twenty-five years, the capitalistic system upon which rests the whole policy of North America, is just^ as antagonistic to the principles of Christianity, of social justice and of British tradition as is the communistic and atheistic system which now prevails in Russia. And for my part I repeat, as a Christian and as a Canadian, I do not consider that we have received either from providence or from the conscience of the Canadian nation any mandate to teach lessons to other nations.
And again, in referring to the atheism which prevailed in France about forty or fifty years ago, the hon. member said:

Did the Conservatives or Liberals of that day, in Canada, suggest that we should break off relations with France and' stop trading with that country because that government was carrying on propaganda against creeds and against religion much more effectively than that carried on during the days of the French revolution, and more effective than that now being carried on by Russia?
And again:

When the delegates from the nations arrived at Genoa, including Mr. Chicherin, one of the primary leaders of the bolshevik government, the venerable Cardinal Archbishop of Genoa received the delegates, including the representative of the government of Russia. The Archbishop shook hands with the delegates and appealed for the blessing of God on their deliberations for peace.

I think the government were wrong four years ago and are right to-day; I think the hon. member for Labelle was right four years ago and wrong this afternoon. I think perhaps the hon. member for Labelle ought to have a greater sense of proportion, perhaps a greater sense of humour. If he would seriously ask a nation that consists in part of Orangemen to drink a loving cup with the Pope perhaps he may permit Mr. Litvinoff to sit in council at a peace table. What did Mr. Litvinoff say on entering the League of Nations? I think possibly his spirit was all that we could very well desire. I should like to read a sentence in which he indicates that apparently he has given up the idea of world revolution and is willing to have Russia go her own way and the other nations their own ways. He said:
The Soviet state has, however, never excluded the possibility of some form or other of association with states having a different political

column1: European Situation-Mr. Woodsworth

and social system, so long as there is no mutual hostility and if it is for the attainment of common aims. For such an association it considers that the essential conditions would be, firstly, the extension to every state belonging to such an association of the liberty to preserve what I might call its state personality and the social-economic system chosen by it-in other words, reciprocal non-interference in the domestic affairs of the states therein associated; and, secondly, the existence of common aims.
Then follows the passage which was quoted by the hon. member for Labelle:

The Soviet union is entering into the league to-day as representative of a new social-economic system, not renouncing any of its special features, and-like the other states here represented'-preserving intact its personality.
And again:

Finally, we must realize once and for all that no war with political or economic aims is capable of restoring so-called historical justice, and that all it could do would be to substitute new and perhaps still more glaring injustices for old ones, and that every new peace treaty bears within it the seeds of fresh warfare.
And again:

I am convinced that in this, our common work, from now on the will to peace of the Soviet union with its 170 million inhabitants -peace for itself and for other states-will make itself felt as a powerful factor.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to pass on for a few moments to what I have already called the danger spots of Germany and Japan. With regard to Germany, I detest Hitlerism and Fascism I think as much as anyone, but I do submit that we, that is the allies, to a very large extent have been responsible for the development of that form of government and that policy in Germany. A few days ago I quoted a paragraph from Mr. Lloyd George, as written September 19, 1932. This so well summarized the position that I venture to give it again:

When the German delegates displayed natural hesitation about accepting these conditions, which reduced their fatherland to impotence in an armed world, Clemenceau wrote them a letter, on behalf and at the request of his colleagues, assuring the Germans that their disarmament would be treated as a prelude to steps for general reduction of armaments by the other nations.
This pledge is also expressed in the covenant of the League of Nations. It was accepted by all the signatories of the treaty and ratified by their senates.

Two of the four who drafted that solemn undertaking have passed away, Clemenceau and Wilson. Signor and I remain. As one of the two survivors, I have no hesitation in accepting the German view that the victorious nations have shamelessly broken faith on the question of armaments. I should be surprised to hear that my co-survivor, Orlando took a different view of the turpitude of the victors in this respect.

The Germans revolt against unscrupulous agitators and designing militarists. Statesmen, of the Fatherland have for thirteen years shown a degree of patience, forbearance and restraint which is worthy of the great people they represented. Throughout this period, the bond they entered into in an hour of crushing defeat was being enforced relentlessly against Germany and her allies, whilst other parties to the contract insolently refused even to discuss performances of their part of the agreement.

I am glad that we may look forward once more to Germany being regarded as a nation on an equality with other nations. I could have -hoped that this might have been accomplished by the reduction of our armaments to the level allowed to Germany. However since Germany has taken strong action and decided she will rearm, I hope it will not be very long before other nations will urge Germany to reenter the League of Nations and that this may be in fact, as some British observers think, the preliminary step to a general disarmament.

May I now say a few words regarding Japan. Last year, on February 12, I outlined briefly the unsatisfactory action taken by Canada in connection with the Manchurian incident. While I have a very high personal regard for the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan)

I think he made a serious mistake in following as apparently he did, the lead of Sir John Simon. I recall asking a question of the government concerning this matter and being told by the Prime Minister that as the matter was sub judice it could not be discussed. In my opinion that was an absolutely absurd position for any government to take. At that time we had an opportunity to take a position that might have had far reaching and worth while results. With regard to Mr. Cahan's speech, the correspondent of Headway, the journal of the British League of Nations Union, wrote:

Twenty-three supported the thesis of the Lytton report, including France and Italy ... three, Japan, Britain and Canada, sympathized with Japan. Canada in a curious oration spoke strongly on both sides.
Professor Soward, writing in Interdependence-the journal of the League of Nations Society in Canada-for March, 1933, made this devastating criticism:

A speech which never once endorsed directly league principles, which departed from our position of last March, which singled out the injured party for most of the recrimination. ... Mr. Cahan's attitude is not the sort which Mr. Meighen assumed at the imperial conference of 1921 when the renewal of the Anglo-Japanese alliance came before the conference.
At that time hon. members will recall it was the stand taken by Canada which to a considerable extent was responsible for the
European Situation-Mr. Woodsworth
refusal of Great Britain to renew the alliance. Professor Soward continues:

When soft words were spoken in Geneva in December the only effect produced was the advance of Japanese troops into Jehol in January. Let our delegate make it clear that we stand for the sanctity of treaties, the maintenance of the collective system and the principles of redress proposed in the Lytton report. As Lord Lytton has well said the league of nations is the life-line of western civilization. Let it not be said that Canada helped to fray its strands. Our government must declare where we stand.

The consequence of Great Britain's lack of Tesolute' action has since been manifest in Japan's aggressive policy. It seems to me that before the close of this debate the government should give some report concerning the work of the advisory committee instructed to follow the developments of the Sino-Japanese situation. Canada is a member of that advisory committee. With regard to the present situation in the east may I quote a paragraph from the observations of the Most Hon. the Marquess of Lothian appearing in an article in International Affairs of March-April, 1935:

Let me now turn to the difficulties of the British position. I do not want to discuss the Manchukuo incident, but Great Britain was certainly not in the front rank in maintaining the collective system in the Pacific at that time. Mr. Stimson was much more forward in the matter than we were. I have always thought that the mistake of British policy at that time was not the view which it took of Japan's intentions in Manchuria-I think its diagnosis ' was closer to the realities than that of the United States-but in its rejection of Mr. Stimson's offer to reverse the isolationist decision of 1920 and act with us in support of the collective system in the Pacific.

There is no doubt at all that the entrance of Russia into the League of Nations has tremendously complicated the entire situation and opened vistas of trouble which Great Britain may confront and which we, as a member of the league, may not altogether avoid.

I should like to quote a paragraph or two from a summary of the situation as contained in a pamphlet Why the U.S.S.R. Joined the League, issued by the New Fabian Research Bureau, with an introduction by Hugh Dalton. The extract follows:

The report of the league assembly, by which Great Britain is bound, declares that (a) Manchuria is an integral part of China, under Chinese sovereignty, and that the nine-power treaty applies to Manchuria as to every other part of China; (b) ""Manchukuo"" is a creation of the Japanese army of occupation which is contrary to the wishes of the inhabitants, and to the interests of China, constitutes a violation of the covenant, nine-power treaty, and the Briand-Kellogg pact, and is incompatible

with the maintenance of peace in the far east; (c) the Japanese military occupation is a result of external aggression for which China bears no responsibility, and is a standing violation of China's territorial integrity and political independence.

What obligations are thereby imposed under the covenant upon any state bound by the assembly report of February 24, 1933, becomes a question of very great importance. It is clear that such a state cannot regard Japan as acting defensively in any war in which she fight9 with China (or with states acting on behalf of the league) to maintain her occupation of China's four northeastern provinces, since that occupation was in breach of the covenant. Owing to the failure of the great powers to defend China, and the covenant, against Japanese aggression an extremely obscure and dangerous situation has been created. It is conceivable that China, and with China some other member of the league acting in the fulfilment of their duties under Articles 10 and 16, may become involved in war with Japan over her occupation of Manchuria.
May I point out that although Canada's obligations under articles 10 and 16 may not be as great as those of Great Britain, they cannot be disregarded.

In that ease it would be the duty of the other member states to treat Japan as the aggresor and the council would have to act immediately under Articles 10 and 16 and advise upon the means by which the obligations of the articles should be fulfilled. It is improbable that the U.S.S.R. or any other state will attempt by independent action to terminate Japan's military occupation. What is more probable is that Japan, as the next step in her present policy, will use Manchuria as a base for invading eastern Siberia. In that case the U.S.S.R. will invoke Article 16. China will become involved on her side, and the other members of the league will be bound by the interpretation given to the covenant and nine-power treaty in the assembly report of February 24. 1933. to treat Japan as the aggressor. For that report has made of Japan in Manchuria an outlaw on Chinese territory, and if peace is restored again the league cannot a second time evade its duty of restoring a situation compatible with the covenant.

BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,,,Mr. Speaker, in rising to offer a few observations on the motion before the house may I at the outset compliment the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) upon the lucid, forcible and comprehensive manner in which he discussed the motion now before the house. While I am in accord with the
European Situation-Mr. Guthrie

principle of the motion I must express entire dissent from many of the views and opinions expressed by the hon. member this afternoon during the course of his remarks. I think we realize that up to the present time we have been engaged largely in a discussion of world affairs and world diplomacy as carried on by the various nations in the world, and I am sure that I express the unanimous opinion of members in every part of the house when I say that it is very deeply regretted that at the present moment the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett) is unable to be in the house to take part in this important discussion. I think the whole house will agree that the Prime Minister's wonderful grasp and understanding of problems of this nature would be invaluable at the present time, that his marked ability in analysing, in portraying and discussing intricate and involved matters would be of the greatest benefit to the house; but perhaps most valuable of all would be the courageous manner in which he is able to consider a difficult question and speedily reach a correct and definite conclusion upon it.

This motion comes before the house to-day by way of an amendment to the motion to go into supply. Under ordinary circumstances such an amendment constitutes a vote of want of confidence in the government, but following precedents established in this house from time to time, in the view of the government, and I fancy in the view of all members of this house, a motion of this kind should not be rejected but should be accepted, if possible, with unanimous approval; and if that be done, as I hope it may be done with regard to this motion, then the house can subsequently go into supply following the practice established by the house upon former occasions.

I have expressed my personal regret at the absence of the Prime Minister at this moment. While I yield to no man in the strong convictions I hold in regard to world peace and the kindred subject of world disarmament, I realize my own limitations and I regret my inability to add very much by way of useful information or cogent argument in support of the motion which has been so elaborately presented to the house this afternoon. As I intimated at the outset I expressly dissent from many of the opinions and views of the mover of this resolution (Mr. Bourassa), but with the principle expressed in the motion I am in most hearty accord. It is a matter of congratulation and of gratification not only in this house but throughout Canada that upon this question, both in this chamber and I fancy also in the upper chamber, there
fMr. Guthrie.]

is and will be but a single opinion, and that opinion favourable. My hon. friend from Labelle did not need to labour the matter so far as the parliament of Canada is concerned or so far as the people of Canada are concerned. He will find the same unanimity throughout Canada upon this question as he will find in the parliament of Canada. Many generations will come and go in this country before the memories of the last great war are obliterated. Our memories are too recent, our trials were too great, our wounds and our injuries too serious, and our burdens still too heavy upon us to allow that great war to pass into the realm of history for many, many years to come. So my hon. friend from Labelle will I think find but a single opinion in regard to future world wars, or in regard to the kindred subject of world1 disarmament.

So far as the national side of this question is concerned there will be little difficulty; there will be but a single opinion. But there is an. international aspect to the subject which must not be forgotten. I doubt if it is possible for any nation in the world at this date to occupy a position of isolation or aloofness without having regard to what is going on in the rest of the world1. Geographical remoteness no longer exists. Time and space have been almost annihilated by modern means of communication and transportation.

BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,,,I do not quite catch the meaning of my hon. friend's remark, but I have made .my statement. In my opinion from now on we will have to assume an international view of many questions which a few years ago we considered as entirely foreign to the interests of Canada, and we shall have to continue to do so in future years, and all nations in the world will be compelled to do the same. We can no longer consider a question such as the subject matter of this motion as purely a national one upon which there is only a single opinion.

I suppose the starting point of our international relationships was in reality the great war. Certainly they arose when we became parties to the treaty of Versailles. We then definitely assumed international obligations. We entered upon international covenants and agreements, and from that day until the
European Situation-Mr. Guthrie
present we have continued so to do. The new position has now become a 'permanent one for the Dominion of Canada.

Let us start with the treaty of Versailles. I do not propose to discuss it but merely to mention some of the subsidiary agreements which have sprung from it and which I find in my discussions in the house and outside are not any too well understood by many people in the Dominion of Canada.

It will be within the memory of a'll, I think that under section 14 of the treaty of Versailles the establishment of a permanent court of international justice was contemplated, and such a court was actually established in the year 1920. Canada became a party to the establishment of that court; so did Great Britain, and so did all the self-governing dominions of the British empire, and all' or nearly all of the nations which had signed the treaty of Versailles. That court was established at The Hague under the auspices of the League of Nations, and was established for the express purpose of settling international disputes of a legal nature, or as stated in the treaty, of a justiciable nature, as opposed to disputes of a political nature. The submission of such disputes was placed upon a purely voluntary basis; there was nothing of a compulsory nature in the original proposal.

This system did not prove entirely satisfactory and' in 1928 another system generally referred to as the optional clause, was evolved under the auspices of the League of Nations. What was this optional clause? It merely removed the voluntary feature and made the submission compulsory as between those states which accepted or acceded1 to the optional clause. Canada, the other British dominions, Great Britain and forty-seven other states in the world acceded to the optional clause and permitted themselves to be bound by a treaty which provides that all disputes of a legal nature between states should be compulsorily referred to The Hague tribunal for final adjustment. There were certain limitations with regard to this submission. I have them here in concise form, and I shall put them on Hansard.

Briefly stated, jurisdiction was conferred upon the international court in respect to all or any classes of legal disputes concerning (a) the interpretation of a treaty; (b) any question of international law; (c) the existence of any fact which if established would constitute a breach of an international obligation, and (d) the nature or extent of reparation to be made for a breach of an international obligation. There are some

other special reservations, one dealing with disputes with regard to questions which by international law fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada. This refers to such matters as fishery questions and so on. I have outlined the matters which might be submitted compulsorily to The Hague tribunal for adjudication. Canada acceded to the optional clause and became bound by it along with forty-seven other nations.

Then followed what is known as the General Act, a most important enactment which, although referred to by this name, is really only a protocol or treaty arising out of the treaty of Versailles. The important provision of the General Act is that all disputes of every nature shall be submitted to the tribunal at The Hague for settlement by that tribunal. The General Act deals not only with legal disputes but with disputes of every nature. Canada acceded to the General Act and agreed to its provisions; so did Great Britain, so did the other self-governing dominions, with the exception of South Africa, and I believe eighteen or twenty of the other leading nations of the world.
The Permanent Court of International Justice was now clothed with these important powers and was accepted by a large proportion of the important nations of the world.
column2: In connection with the optional

column1: clause we find that it was acceded to by France, Great Britain, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Holland, Austria, Hungary, and the British dominions. If a dispute were to arise between Canada and any of these nations, such dispute would automatically go to the international court for settlement. How is a settlement arrived at? The first provision for settlement is by way of conciliation; if that fails, then by arbitration if the parties agree; if that fails, then finally by the judgment of the court itself which is reported to the League of Nations.

This court has proved of inestimable advantage during the ten or twelve years of its existence. There have been from 470 to 480 references made to the court in connection with treaties and agreements and differences between nations. Many notable disputes have been adjudicated upon and finally settled. In addition to this, the League of Nations has the power to refer to the court for an opinion any involved questions which may arise from time to time, and I believe the court has already rendered between thirty and forty opinions in this connection. We in Canada deliberately

column1: European Situation^-Mr. Guthrie
acceded to all these protocols to ensure the peace of Canada and the peace of the world, so did all the other nations which accepted these treaties and acceded to the court.

The only other treaty which I desire to mention at this time is the one which was discussed so ably this afternoon by the hon. member for Labelle, the treaty known as the pact of Paris, the treaty of Paris, or, perhaps more generally, the Briand-Kellogg pact. I believe this treaty was originally framed by the government of the United States. It was submitted to the government of Prance, the details were finally settled and it was placed before the nations of the world and their adherence to its provisions requested. This treaty was signed in Paris in 1928 and formally adopted by the parliament of Canada the following spring. It received the approval of and the adoption by no less than sixty nations of the world. The provisions of this treaty were outlined quite fully this afternoon and I need refer to it only very briefly.

The first clause of the treaty condemns recourse to war and declares that war shall be renounced as a means of settlement of international disputes. Surely that language is plain and distinct and any nation which signed the treaty should readily understand it. Clause two is just as plain and just as distinct; it provides that all international disputes shall be settled by pacific means. These brief provisions constitute the treaty of Paris. It is a plain and explicit enactment accepted by sixty nations of the world. I remember hearing the treaty of Paris criticized on one occasion by an American lawyer who stated that one of its weaknesses lay in the fact that no sanctions were provided, that there was no means of enforcing it. The only means of enforcing such a treaty is through the influence of world opinion, and I doubt if any signatory to the treaty would, except for very cogent reasons, deviate from its provisions having in mind the tremendous adverse world opinion which would immediately ensue. It is rather discouraging that notwithstanding the covenants, the protocols, the treaties and the agreements, during recent years two of the signatories to the treaty of Paris engaged in open warfare. I refer to China and Japan. It is discouraging also when we look at Europe to-day and consider the case of Italy and Abyssinia or the general situation which obtains throughout the continent of Europe. It is discouraging also that in spite of all these pacts and treaties and leagues and covenants, that there are more armed men in the world to-day than at the outbreak of the war in 1914, and also that there are greater armaments in the world to-day than there were in
1914. Such is the condition which confronts the world to-day.

The motion moved by my hon. friend from Labelle is exceedingly appropriate to the present situation, and I trust that I shall not give offence to the hon. gentleman if I make a few comments on the argument which he addressed to the House of Commons to-day.

He made it quite plain today, that he does not approve either the diplomacy or the actions of some British statesmen in the great effort to assure the peace of the world.",,,,

BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,RTTISKD EDITION,,I think the hon. member's whole attitude in regard to the League of Nations and the statement he made this afternoon clearly shows, that he was running true to form in respect of this matter. The halfhearted praise with which he damned the League of Nations, the grudging support which he gave it-and everyone in this chamber realized that it was merely grudging support-made no appeal to me.
fMr. Guthrie.]
There is this to be said about the League of Nations and Canada's part in it:
column2: Canada

column1: has consistently supported the league since its inception; there has not been a meeting of the assembly of that august body at which Canadians have not been present to represent their country, and it is a matter of pride to Canadians; it is a matter of pride to me that in 1925 Senator Dandurand was elected president of the assembly of the league, and also that in 1927 he represented Canada on the council of the league, the council being, as the house knows, the power house of the league. Canada has won a high place in the council of the league. But we must not overestimate the influence of this country in a gathering such as meets annually at Geneva, consisting of some forty, fifty or sixty of the great nations of the world. I know and they know that Canada is a country of ten million people, a new nation. I have been there myself on one occasion, and we all realize when we go there that the influence of Canada is respected, but I would not say that it is great; certainly it is not predominant in any way. But consistently Canada has supported at the gathering of the league all measures for world peace and all measures for world disarmament.

There is this to be said, that during its career of some fourteen or fifteen years the league has been a very steadying influence in world affairs. It may not have succeeded in keeping down all armed conflict, but it has succeeded in settling many difficult problems which might otherwise have caused revolt throughout the world had the good auspices of the league not been employed in the settlement of them. One of the weaknesses of the league, one of the weaknesses of the permanent court at The Hague, lies in the fact that the United States has not become a party to either of them. Another weakness, when I was there, arose from the fact that Russia had not become a party to the league. I for one, expressing my own opinion, am gratified to know that Russia now belongs to the league. I may say that in 1931 when I attended as a representative from this country, Canada was the only nation in North America that was a member of the league. I was asked to say a word in support of the application of Mexico to join the league. It was the first occasion on which I made a speech in that body; I was very glad to endorse the application and Mexico became a member at that gathering. Not that I have any tremendous respect for Mexico; I know very little about it, but I think it is far better for the peace of the world that countries like Russia and
European Situation-Miss Macphail
Mexico should belong to the league and come under its influence than that they should remain outside it.

I do not know that I have anything further to add in regard to this matter. To my mind Canada's duty is clear; we should pursue the even tenor of our ways; we should seek to mould and control public opinion as far as possible in support of all peace proposals and international disarmament. Canada is recognized at Geneva as one of the fow countries in the world where armaments are considered negligible. We are in no sense of the word an armed nation. I believe our expenditure on armaments upon a per capita basis is lower than that of any of the other civilized countries. That is one example which we have set at Geneva, but it is not an example which has prevailed upon the other nations to limit their armaments. Whether limitation can be accomplished, whether disarmament will become an accomplished fact in the near future, one cannot say. Our efforts, our hopes and our prayers are directed in support of disarmament. We hope our prayers may be answered; but let us continue to pursue the course we have followed for the last ten years, the active support of all peace proposals. I do not believe the time has yet come when men are prepared to beat their swords into ploughshares, their spears into pruning hooks. That day may be yet far distant, but Canada's [DOT] course is plain.

There is nothing in the principle involved in this motion to which I could object; I accept it as it is drawn and so does the government. I cannot however accept the statements made in regard to it by the hon. member for Labelle. I approve in every way the League of Nations. I can only say that if it can succeed in keeping the peace of the world; if it can succeed in driving the fear of war from the minds of men and in removing the burdens of war from the backs of weary multitudes, it will accomplish much in the cause of civilization.

Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Before the question is put, Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity of agreeing with the position taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) this afternoon and evening. I think the hon. member expressed, as well as another could, my views on a constructive national policy for Canada.

I do not intend to express again the numerous positive, emphatic statements the hon. member made in the stand that he felt, as a typical Canadian, he should take. As I followed almost all the speeches that have

been made on this subject I felt that the outstanding causes of war boiled down to possibly two. In the first place I think there are unnatural boundaries which outrage the ideas of racial solidarity and ignore the cultural rights of minorities, and I believe these unnatural boundaries are very largely the result of the treaty of Versailles. For many years I have been out of sympathy with that treaty; I think it contains the causes of many wars. Whether or not we shall be able to change the treaty in time to save the world from those wars I do not know.

The other cause of war, which to me seems by far the chief cause, is the ever increasing, bitter fight for diminishing markets. I believe I have expressed my feeling in almost the same words previously during this session. Every country in the world is seeking to sell in the markets of the world those goods which their own people would -like so much to have but which they cannot afford to buy. When you find every country seeking to sell surplus goods in the world markets, with no one wishing to buy, there is bound to be increasing competition. Not only do nations seek to sell; every country seems to believe that it must have a surplus of sales over purchases, or what we call a favourable trade balance. Any reasonable person knows that every country cannot have a favourable balance of trade; it is impossible. A few countries may have such a balance, but all countries cannot have it, and this frightful effort on the part of every nation to sell more than it buys-which of course is impossible-has helped bring the world to the state of tension in which it finds itself at the moment.

There are, of course, very many other factors. I do believe that when armaments multiply rapidly they are not only an indication of war but are a cause of war. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) spoke-of the court of international settlement, and I think everyone is glad that so many causes of war have been referred to that court. But may I say that the chief causes of war are of such a nature that they cannot be referred to the permanent court of international settlement, or as the United States call it, the world court. That is true in regard to this ever-increasing struggle for markets. That is not a .matter that can be referred to the court of international settlement, and in my, opinion those matters which can be referred to the court, are not the chief causes of war. I think they are minor matters and that the chief cause of war is this frightful struggle for markets which, as conditions are to-day, really do not exist. That matter will not and indeed cannot be referred to the court of international settlement,

column2: COMMONS

column1: European Situation-Miss Macphail

so while I am glad we have the court and I am glad of its success up to this time, I do not think we can look to it with any real confidence as a tribunal that will settle the most aggravated causes of war.

I feel more and more that we must learn to distribute goods and services in every country up to the needs of the people, and when we have satisfied the people's needs in each country, the terrific struggle for markets will be lessened by exactly the amount of goods consumed by the people who to-day are living below a decent standard.

This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that when he was at a meeting of the league he formed the impression that Europe played too important a part in the work of that body. No one who has ever been there could have any other feeling. You feel that Europe takes itself much too: seriously and that unfortunately the world takes Europe much too seriously. After all Europe is only one continent and there are many others, but the league is dominated by the European nations and European problems, and there has not been anything like sufficient recognition of other continents and their problems. Today no thoughtful person can look at even the headlines in the daily papers without being deeply troubled or without seeing that in spite of all the talk of peace the nations are making frantic efforts to rearm. If ever there was a time when Canadians needed to take their place in the League of Nations seriously, that time is now. Much as I would like to think that Canada has taken her work in connection with the League of Nations seriously, I must disagree with the opinion of the Minister of Justice in that regard. I think we have taken a very nominal place there; I think we could have done very much better if we had taken our work in connection with the league more seriously. That is a subject in connection with which I have stated my position previously.

There is one other matter to which I should like to refer, and that is in connection with the things we might do right here in Canada. I do feel that one way of improving Canada's work in connection with the league is to have the portfolio of external affairs held by a minister other than the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is too busy; he cannot leave Canada as often as is necessary to discharge, most efficiently the duties in connection with that portfolio, and I think the change should be made without delay. Then we have in Canada an organization that is seeking to do a very fine piece of

work in educating public opinion, and that is doing its work very well indeed when one considers the meagre funds at its disposal; I refer to the League of Nations Society. I do not believe the House of Commons of Canada can say conscientiously that it is working for peace when it votes to the League of Nations Society in Canada only $3,000. When certain subscriptions to League of Nations documents are paid the net amount is only about $2,000. The parliament of Canada votes only $2,000 to the League of Nations Society but votes millions for military equipment. We maintain a military college. In the present year we have heard of some fairly large contributions to the Boy Scouts Association. I have no fault to find with the Boy Scouts, but I believe there can be very little comparison, so far as the good which can be accomplished is concerned, between the Boy Scouts Association and the League of Nations Society in Canada. Before dissolution we ought to vote to the League of Nations Society in Canada a sum of money in keeping with its importance and with the very intelligent work it is doing.

There are many functions the society could perform but which on account of shortage of funds it finds impossible to perform. I do not wish it to become a creature of the government or of parliament, but I do say the moneys the society collects by way of subscriptions and donations ought to be liberally supplemented by a vote of this parliament. Had they the money I believe they could supervise intelligently an extensive peace program to extend throughout the dominion. They could do much towards linking up the work in Canada with that of international institutions outside the dominion which are working in the interests of the people. They could do much through existing organizations such as farm and labour groups, schools and churches, to inform the people on international matters. They could cooperate with the press and with women's organizations. They could have a panel of well informed and well trained speakers; they could have literature, posters, and so on.

Some years ago I suggested in this chamber that scholarships should be provided1 whereby it would be possible for Canadian students to go abroad on a more extensive scale than now obtains, and students of other countries to come to Canada to study. I still believe that might well be done. Last year and indeed for many years I attended the annual meeting of the League of Nations
_________European Situation-Mr. Mackenzie King

Society in Canada. I wish every hon. member could have attended it, because the annual meeting held last May at the Chateau Laurier was an intellectual treat. The papers and discussions were of a nature which it would have profited us to go a long way to hear. The standard was so high that I believe it would be advisable to make arrangements whereby such a society might be in a position financially to arrange for a summer school in which certain subjects could be pursued and possibly certain definite conclusions arrived at. Such a school would be one not of propaganda but of education in the best sense of the term. The League of Nations Society could do a great deal towards encouraging creative thinking in the schools and colleges of Canada along lines of international relationships. My statement may sound ridiculous, but I believe I am correct when I say that if we can support a military college we ought not to claim to be completely devoted to the cause of peace until we are willing to support a peace college, if it could be so termed. At any rate, if we cannot have a separate college every assistance should be given to the departments in colleges already established which are seeking to enlarge the people's knowledge of international relations. The establishment of a peace college may offend some people who might (believe that peace propaganda would be broadcast. However I should be inclined to think it would be a perfectly sound proposition to establish a peace college: and would be no more in the way of propaganda than would a military college such as is already established.

I believe there is a great need in Canada of a library devoted to the subject of international relations and good will. The League of Nations Society need such a library. They have not the money to buy the volumes nor indeed have they sufficient to procure rooms for the bare physical framework of a library. And so I urge-and it is really for this reason I have risen-that we do this thing which lies at our hand. It is something we can do. I think in Professor MacDermot the League of Nations Society has a secretary with the intellectual capacity sufficient to do all the things I have mentioned and many I have not mentioned. I 'believe he is capable of giving intellectual leadership to a peace movement in Canada, and I do feel as members of the House of Commons we should do this very small thing, this one concrete thing.
I again urge that the portfolio of Secretary of State for External Affairs be separated from that of the Prime Minister, and that

such official should head the delegations to the League of Nations Assembly year after year, so that his knowledge of these matters would be comparable with the knowledge of other delegation heads going there from year to year.

In closing I wish to repeat that in my opinion the chief causes of war are economic, and until there is a distribution of goods and services which will allow the people of the world to enjoy the goods which they themselves produce, we will not be eliminating the root causes of war.

MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,SUPPLY-EUROPEAN SITUATION AMENDMENT BY MR. BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,RTTISKD EDITION,,Mr. Speaker, I was greatly impressed by one observation made at the beginning of his address by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). He spoke of the gravity of the situation in Europe, saying that it was one which threatened the peace of the world. Having made that declaration the hon. member then proceeded to express the hope, one which I think was in the breasts of all hon. members, that any debate which might take place would not be in the nature of party controversy. I had hoped that upon this occasion such might prove to be the case. I can see however wherein it was unavoidable that exception should be taken to some of the observations of the hon. member. Indeed I would not be honest with him or with the house if I did not state that while I concur in very much of what he said there were some of his remarks with which I could not agree. May I say however that while hon. members in this chamber may debate these matters in a manner which is understood among themselves and in all parts of our country, in view of the conditions obtaining in Europe to-day, and in view of what is happening even in the present week, there is a danger that some observations made in this chamber, while understood by hon. members and by Canadians, may not be as well understood in other parts of the world. For that reason I believe upon this occasion we cannot be too guarded in our criticisms of events in the old world. There have been negotiations between Britain and Germany; there are negotiations going on between Britain and Russia, and in the course of a few days the negotiations will be enlarged to include other nations of Europe, all with the one great objective of effecting a collective security and maintaining the peace of the world. I submit that there is no question of the day comparable in importance or consequence with the situation as it is existing in Europe to-day. It would be most unfortunate indeed if any

column2: COMMONS

column1: European Situation-Mr. Mackenzie King
word from either side of this house should go out to -the world, the purpose of which was capable of 'being in any way misconstrued.

May I say that I welcome very much the resolution which my hon. friend from Labelle has introduced. I am glad that the government has found it possible to accept the motion wholeheartedly, that they have not found it necessary to discover technical reasons why this motion which is being moved on going into supply cannot be accepted by the government and by the house, and I hope and believe and know that it will be accepted unanimously.

It is at this time quite appropriate that we should reaffirm, and reaffirm very strongly, the position of Canada with respect to the Paris peace pact, as it is termed, the Briand-Kellogg pact, and the position that we in Canada take in relation to the work of the League of Nations. The first clause of the motion, that ""this house reiterates the adhesion of Canada to the general treaty for the renunciation of war signed at Paris on the 27th day of August, 1928, and approved by this house on the 22nd day of February, 1929,"" will I know be acceptable to every hon. member of the house without respect to the party to which he may belong. I am pleased to'recall that in 1928 I had the honour of. signing in Paris the Briand-Kellogg pact on behalf of Canada. We in this parliament have heretofore approved the peace pact, and at this moment it is I think wholly appropriate and perhaps helpful to the world situation that we should reaffirm our endors-ation of it.

There is but one other clause in the motion, and it ""invites the government to lend its support to all effective measures to ensure the world's peace either through the League of Nations or otherwise in cooperation with other governments pledged to the cause of peace."" I hope that every living soul in this country will be prepared to support that clause. I believe they will be. I cannot imagine that in any part of Canada to-day there exists anyone who would desire the government to do other than all that is within its power at a time like this in the world's affairs to further any project that will make for peace and give the utmost support- that it can to any institution that is working for the peace of the world.

It is easy to criticize institutions. The League of Nations, like all other institutions, has its limitations, but after all it is the one continuing consultative international body working for peace in the world to-day. It is the one recognized world agency for the purpose of furthering cooperation among those

nations that are seeking to preserve peace. We can only begin to estimate its value when we ask ourselves what position the world might be in to-day had no such world agency been created, had no public opinion been aroused such as has been aroused and formulated within the last ten or fifteen years through the agency of the League of Nations, and which is making itself felt at the present time.

Only a few months ago the world was horrified by a crime perpetrated at Marseilles. It looked for the moment as if Europe might as a result of that crime be plunged again immediately into war. It recalled to the mind of everyone what happened at Sarajevo shortly before the beginning of the great war. But what has happened since is evidence that while there may be forces which are preparing for war, that are seeking to be in readiness for the moment of action, on the other hand there are other forces which are working very strongly for peace. The forces which are working for peace were able last year at least to prevent that crime being followed by an event so disastrous as that which followed the assassination at Sarajevo. There are many other evidences that the forces which are working for peace have found a means of coordination, have found a method of common expression and a promise of world support through the League of Nations, which would not be present to-day but for the existence of the league.

Certainly so far as Canada is concerned I think that what has been said to-night about our part in the league, modest as it has been, has been well said. The example of Canada, while a small country, has nevertheless been one which other nations as well as we ourselves could point to with pride. The fact that geographically we are situated as we are with a great and powerful nation t-o the south of us, and that our difficulties for a century and more have -been settled by the appeal to reason rather than by the appeal to force affords an object lesson to the world the like of which can only be discovered on this continent. If the countries of Asia and Europe would follow the example of North America and appoint international joint commissions to which their disputes might be referred for consideration and investigation and report, bringing to bear the light of an informed public opinion upon the case in dispute, I venture to say that the need for much in the way of armament would soon disappear.
I repeat that I hardly think in the light of the European situation at the moment and what is being sought to be done to improve
European Situation-Mr. Mackenzie King

conditions there, it is wise to go too far in our discussion of policies that may or may not be best for the' preservation of peace. I would like however, to say with regard to disarmament that I do not think it is sufficient for this country simply to say that it supports the League of Nations in its policy of disarmament. I think we ought to name a concrete policy in that regard. Having observed what has taken place in investigations in the United States, where beyond all question it has been shown that there are those who are prepared to traffic in the manufacture and sale of munitions and armaments for the sake of gain, that there are large interests that are even selling simultaneously to countries that are at enmity with each other, it behooves this country and I believe all nations to begin immediately to investigate the whole business of armament manufacture and sale. I should like to see a beginning made in this country of a thorough investigation into the whole business of the manufacture and sale and distribution of munitions of war and armaments, and that step put forward as part of a policy to govern British countries, a policy that we would hope might be followed in all parts of the British empire. I am glad that in Great Britain a commission has been appointed for the purpose, and I am sure that if the British empire as a whole made it a part of the policy of its several parts to investigate to the utmost limit the workings of these great armament production interests and those who are concerned on the commercial side with the sale of munitions, it would have an enormous effect upon, other countries, and if the United States paralleled the example of the British empire in that regard, that example would soon be followed by other nations of the world with results of benefit to mankind.

I agree with what has been said this evening by the last speaker (Miss Macphail) in her references to the importance of our economic policies, our trade policies as well as those policies that are more immediately associated with the question of war. I believe the greatest curse with which the world has been faced in the last five years has been the curse of economic nationalism. As I have said repeatedly, if there is one curse that is greater it is that of economic imperialism. I believe that the sooner we find a nation which has the courage to set an example to other nations of a friendly attitude in the matter of trade, a friendliness carried to the point of presenting to other countries an opportunity to trade, the sooner we will find a breaking down of those walls behind which hatred between different nations has been fostered.

There is no doubt that the cause of much of the world's unrest which exists to-day is the consciousness that countries are being denied the opportunity of trading with other parts of the world. The idea that a selfish policy of the kind can be fought with retaliation is a serious mistake. Retaliation in kind has only served to make conditions which were bad infinitely worse. A great deal has been said to-day about a Christian attitude in human affairs and in international relations. If we are going to talk about the brotherhood of man, it is about time we began to treat those who belong to other nations as though they were brothers instead of enacting embargoes and prohibitive trade restrictions and other vexatious hindrances to trade. This is one thing which bears upon a condition which we all know to exist in this as well as in other countries of the world.

I am inclined to believe that much good could be done if this and other countries were to take a more definite stand on what they would or would not do in the matter of helping to preserve collective security. TheTe should be more definite statements as to the attitude which would be adopted toward any nation which would threaten the security of other nations or which was proven by the facts to be guilty of having disturbed the peace of the world. I think this country ought to declare that any nation which could be shown to have threatened the peace of the world by violating a pact of collective security should be denied any assistance in the shape of men or munitions, should be denied any assistance in the nature of food, should be denied any assistance through credit. Our country, small as it is, might well lay down a definite policy in that regard as expressing Canada's attitude toward any country which upon the facts being disclosed was found to be guilty of attempting to destroy what otherwise might be collective security. If that example were followed by other parts of the British empire, as I believe it would be, it would soon be followed by other parts of the world.

What I am seeking to emphasize at the moment is the fact that as part of the British empire this country should make itself heard even more definitely than in the past with respect to some of these matters upon which we feel very deeply. I do not believe that a situation could develop in Europe which would engulf that country in war without the effects of that situation inevitably being felt in all quarters of the world. It is quite easy to say that we would stay out of

column2: COMMONS

column1: European Situation-Mr. Mackenzie King

the war, that we would not send men to fight in Europe, but after the experience I had of the pressure which was exerted at the time of the Chanak incident, referred to this afternoon, I have very grave doubts as to what might happen in Canada if war were to break out again in any part of the world. I think we can take it for granted that the next war will not 'be one which however colossal its death and destruction may be, will leave the world simply in depths of depression and distress such as it has experienced in recent years; it will 'be a war which will do much to obliterate human society itself. There cannot be any conceivable menace to mankind as great as that.

When I went to Europe last year I did so largely with the view of ascertaining at first hand the facts with respect to the situation which one was led to .believe existed in the old country. The impression which I gathered from conversations with those who were well informed in Great Britain, France and Italy was that while the peoples of Europe undoubtedly did not wish war, while the governments themselves did not wish war, there was no one who would say that conditions were not such that war might not occur at almost any moment. What has taken place in Europe during the last few years? We all know that much of what there was of democratic institutions before and even since the war has been swept away. Instead of government under democratic methods such as we have under the British parliamentary system, there is in Europe to-day a network of dictatorships. There is a dictatorship in Russia, there is a dictatorship in Germany, in Italy and in Austria as well as in other countries. What happens under a dictatorship is that the will of one man may precipitate an entire country into a step which it becomes impossible to retrieve. So long as communities remain democratic, and so long as governments are subject to the will of members of parliament who are representatives of the people as a whole, I for one have not the least fear of war commencing in those countries. (But where peoples have surrendered their freedom to autocratic governments, where autocratic governments have become more and more government by individuals whose will and whose wish become the expressions of the nations as a whole, then there is an increasingly grave menace to human society.

I believe that the British people will perhaps be able to render their greatest contribution to the world by maintaining their system of government as it has developed during the last century or two. I believe that to-day

Great Britain is wielding a great influence for good in Europe, and is able to wield that influence because it is known throughout Europe that when Great Britain speaks she is speaking for the people of Great Britain as a whole. The trouble with some of the other countries is that when a word is spoken no one can say whether it is the word of the people or of an individual. What perhaps is most serious of all is the fact that contracts have lost their sanctity. The written word, the pledge, has ceased to have the value which it had in years gone by. In Great Britain the written contract is still accepted, and the pledge is still honoured; when the government of Great Britain gives an undertaking it is something which can be relied upon, and I believe the voice of Great Britain speaking in this authoritative way may yet prove to be the voice which will help most to preserve the peace of the world. So far as this parliament is concerned, every hon. member feels I am sure that the greatest service we can render to-day to the peace of the world is to let it be known that so far as the efforts which Great Britain is making are towards mediation, towards conciliation and towards eliminating the fears of nations, the members of all political parties in Canada are unitedly and strongly behind such efforts.

BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,"In

view of the very generous reception with which the budget has met at the hands of the press of Canada, for me to devote any time to complimenting the minister on his presentation would certainly be like carrying
The Budget-Mr. Beynon

coals to Newcastle. Suffice it to say that I feel both satisfied and gratified with the . budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) this year. I was struck with the change in the method of procedure of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). I have always listened with a good deal of interest to his annual onslaught on the budget and I listened again this year with equal interest.
I noticed, however, this year for the first time that he spent practically half an hour in what I might term amusing witticisms.

It is the first time he has blossomed forth as a humorist, and I do not think that the hon. gentleman is as happy in that role as he is in the role of a serious critic. I think we all felt that his humour was perhaps a little too premeditated; it never surprised us-we always anticipated it. The hon. gentleman might be pardoned for making that departure this year inasmuch as the Minister of Finance had left him a very difficult task, and it was quite natural that he should attempt to cover with levity his failure to find at least one vulnerable spot in the budget.

The hon. gentleman's first attack was upon the policies of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) when he went to the old country in connection with the economic conference. My hon. friend revived the old story, that the Prime Minister, by his ""blasting"" policies, had offended the British people and made it impossible for us to trade with other countries. I should have thought that this would be a very inopportune time for the hon. member to bring up that question. He must surely remember that his right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) went to the old country the latter part of last year and undoubtedly sounded the British people as to their attitude towards these agreements, and on his return to this country he precipitated a family quarrel in the Liberal party by ordering the mighty Vincent to destroy tons of literature he had prepared in denunciation of the agreements. I should think the charred remains of that pile of campaign ammunition would be a silent reminder that a false statement remains a false statement, no matter how often it is repeated.

The next charge he made against us was that we had led the way in economic nationalism and now we are recanting. Surely the hon. gentleman knows the difference between recognizing a fact and espousing a principle. All this government and the Prime Minister have done is to recognize the fact that

economic nationalism is rampant in the . world, but to say that this government or the Prime Minister has adopted that as a principle is far from the fact. On the contrary the very statement made by the right hon. leader of the opposition contradicts the idea, for he said that the Prime Minister's attitude was to blast his way into the markets of the world. Surely that is absolutely at variance with the idea of economic nationalism.

The next charge he has to make against us is that we have failed to keep the channels of trade open. I am not going to reiterate what has been stated so often in the house or to deal further with a matter so ably dealt with by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) in his reply. Surely if there is anything in which the Liberal party has excelled, it is in repeating over and over again a statement hon. members opposite know is not true and doing so without batting an eye. It has been repeated in the house and throughout the country; it has been stated by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) and nearly all speakers on this side, that almost every market in the world was closed to our products before this government came into power. One cannot help admiring the persistence and audacity of people who will, in the face of what has been said, continue to reiterate that this government has closed the markets of the world to' Canada.

Then the hon. member attacked the basis of our trade balance; he said that we prided ourselves on our favourable trade balance but that it is not of the value we claim because, he said, it was not properly obtained; it was obtained by .restricting imports instead oif by increasing exports. Well, it changed from a favourable trade balance to an adverse one of some $140,000,000 or $150,000,000 during the regime of hon. members opposite. If that is so, did they keep the channels of trade open? Did they keep our exports up? Surely if we had an adverse trade balance of $140,000,000 and a favourable one is desirable, as they are prepared to admit it is provided it is obtained in the right way, the time was opportune for them to proceed to obtain that favourable trade balance by increasing exports, which he says is the proper way to do it. It therefore follows that the hon. gentleman's party has failed to do the very thing which he has charged us with failing to do. What happened? Canada, being a debtor nation, must have a favourable trade balance or
The Budget-Mr. Beynon
must face bankruptcy, if she cannot obtain a favourable trade balance by increasing exports, then she must obtain it in some other way. What this government did was to obtain it in two ways:
column2: first, by decreasing

column1: imports and, second, by increasing exports. But this government recognized the fact, which apparently the previous government did not do, that this country, being a debtor nation, would face bankruptcy if it did not have a favourable trade balance.

I want to remind the house that in 1914 this world faced I suppose the most tragic crisis in its history. At that time it needed men of ability, of education, with trained minds and force of character, as leaders in the armies of the world. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth volunteered his services, and I am glad to say that he proved to be a very valuable, efficient and loyal soldier. A gratified nation wished to recognize the services he was performing, the sacrifice he was making in devoting himself to the service of his country. He went overseas as a major; he was promoted t*o the rank of lieutenant-colonel; he was given a substantial remuneration for his services while overseas, although perhaps not what everybody would think was sufficient, but all that the nation could afford under the circumstances. He was decorated; he was given marks of distinction, of honour; he was mentioned in dispatches. He was admitted into the best society of the land; he was wined, dined and feasted. He was given a batman to brush his clothes, polish his shoes and shine his buttons, saving him from all menial tasks. In fact everything that could be done for him was done in recognition of the valuable service he was rendering to his country. Moreover, he was given immunity from political aspersion. People were not allowed to say that the hon. member in his work as a soldier was fighting not for his country but for his own glory. He was immune from that because the people would not permit such things to be said of a man who was giving himself to his country. The war crisis ended.

Twelve years rolled by and another crisis arose. This however Was a peace crisis, almost as bad, a tragedy perhaps as deep and dark as ony of those met with on the fields of Flanders. Again we required men of training and ability, men who were willing to sacrifice themselves for their country. In western Canada we had such a man in the person of John I. McFarland, who volunteered his services. He had a peculiarly trained mind. But what did the country do for him? It is brae a private corporation offered him a salary, but he refused it. He was not given
a uniform; he was not given any medals ,or badges or award. He was not given a batman; he was not given any rank of distinction, not even that of a corporal. He was not wined, dined or feasted.

BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,but in the quiet of a drab, dull depression in which there is absolutely nothing in the way of glory or glamour but only the opportunity to serve his fellow Canadians. Yet the hon. member for Slhel-bume-Yarmouth was not generous enough to refrain from casting such aspersions.

It is possible, of course, that the hon. member does not fully appreciate the tragedy that is being enacted on those western plains. He is living in the midst of a large city, in the more or less fortified recesses of St. James street, where matters of this kind cannot be fully understood or appreciated. At the same time I submit that before making a charge of this kind against a man like Mr. McFarland he should more thoroughly investigate these matters. It is true that on several occasions the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) has made similar statements, which have been passed by without a great deal of thought or without a great deal of attention being paid to them. Perhaps that is due1 to the fact that oh this side of the house it is not generally thought that the hon. member for Willow Bunch is capable of anything better, but we did expect something better from the hon. member for Shelburne-
Yarmouth. He is a soldier, a scholar and a gentleman, and we expected something better of him.

What are the criticisms that are' levelled against Mr. McFarland? The first is that in 1933 he either did not sell the wheat, or if he did he went into the market and bought it back again. Let us just examine that for a moment, because it indicates very clearly that the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth does not really understand very much about the wheat business,. As a matter of fact every time Mr. McFarland sold a quantity of wheat he stepped right into the market and bought that quantity of wheat back again by way of options. That was necessary; it was impossible for Mr. McFarland to sell any wheat without doing that, for the simple reason, that neither the millers nor the exporters will buy any wheat at- all unless they can hedge their purchases, and Mr. McFarland was taking the hedges. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth seems to think that if Mr. McFarland goes in the market and sells one thousand, ten thousand, or one hundred thousand bushels of wheat, that amount immediately disappears from the world's surplus. It does not matter whether that wheat is in Winnipeg, on the boat or in England; until it is manufactured into flour and sold to the consumer it is still a part of the world's surplus. There is no such thing as stepping into the market and disposing of this carry-over or this surplus of ours overnight.

What is the next statement of the hon. gentleman? He says the government of this country is holding the price, of wheat in western Canada far too high, and by reason of that fact we are losing the, British market. I want it to be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that every Liberal member from western Canada applauded that statement when it was made in this house and they are all committed to that statement of fact and that principle, that the government is holding the price of wheat in western Canada too high. The people of the west must remember that if hon. gentlemen opposite are returned to power naturally they will immediately proceed to correct that which they believe to be wrong; the people of the west must remember that if hon. gentlemen opposite come into power the price of wheat will go down. How is that to be accomplished? It can be done only by throwing all the wheat on the market regardless of price, and that is the policy advocated by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth. He said, ""Why didn't he sell it; why not throw it on the market
The Budget-Mr. Beynon

and let the price go down, as the Argentine and Australia did?"" What would have been the result? If that policy had been followed there could have been only one result; you would have had practically the entire population of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta on relief. In addition you would have lost at least $25,000,000 of purchasing power in Canada; there would have been much more to be raised in the way of taxes in the east and there would have been much less goods purchased in the east and consequently less money with which to pay those taxes. So you would have had something like economic chaos in Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite are sometimes wont to laugh when the Prime Minister speaks of having spent his days and nights trying to maintain the industrial and financial structure of this country. I want to say that one of the big aids in maintaining that industrial and financial structure was the support given by this government to the grain market.

The hon. member says we are losing our grain markets, that England is ceasing to trade with us and that if they come into power they will throw the grain on the market and depress the price to the point where the British millers will buy it. To show that this is actually the Liberal policy I have before me a quotation from the Winnipeg Free Press, which after all is the mouthpiece of the Liberal party in western Canada. In 1920 the Winnipeg Free Press had a certain policy with respect to wheat, and this is what it was:

Since July enormous quantities of low priced wheat have been exported to Europe from the Argentine, Liverpool buyers were under no necessity to buy Canadian wheat at $1.59 per bushel or thereabouts, when they could buy from Argentine at $1.12.
On October 23, 1929, there appeared the following editorial:

In such a situation with more wheat offering to buyers than they want, the argument that Canadian wheat should be freely offered at competitive prices seems curious. If it were thrown on the market at prices which made it highly attractive to speculators, it might be bought, but would it be used? The price might fall, and the wheat still remain in storage.
Further on they say:
Whatever the economic effect has been this summer in the Argentine, the fact is that Argentine wheat is being sold at prices in Liverpool which would be disastrous to Canadian producers.

I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that at the time this editorial was written for the Winnipeg Free Press, Argentine wheat was selling at $1.12 a bushel. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite tell us to-day, at a time when
Argentine wheat is selling from 50 cents to 60 cents per bushel, that we should dump our wheat on the market in competition with that wheat, and that the western farmer should take the consequences.

We see that a little later the Free Press, as usual, had a change of heart. In 1929 the Liberal party was responsible for the government, but in 1935 we have a Conservative government. Criticizing the speech made by Mr. McFarland in Moose Jaw they have this to say about the wheat situation:
The next most significant feature of Mr. McFarland's address was his attempt to return to 1929 conditions and the mentality of that year.
Here is a very significant statement:
Of course, everybody was wrong about wheat in 1929.
The Free Press admits it was wrong about wheat in 1929.

We were all at that time warm with enthusiasm over our belief that the world had to come to us for wheat and that the price would be what we chose to demand. But people capable of learning were pretty thoroughly cured by the experiences of that year. As the season of 1929 advanced, it was revealed to our chagrin that the world's statistical position of wheat was not what we fondly thought it was; that the domestic crops in European countries were far larger than estimated; and that there was literally no end to the supplies of wheat from Argentine. The lesson that 1929 should have taught us was that if in competitive markets our wheat is held above the current price, we keep the wheat (which bulges forth as a carry-over) and the other nations do the business.

That sets forth the position of the Liberal party to-day. That is what the Free Press has been advocating for the last year and a half, namely, that we throw this wheat upon the market and let the price be depressed to whatever point it may, letting the western farmer take the loss. What have the western producers to do?

I was amused when the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth mentioned he was going to speak for a while on behalf of the western farmers. One of the first statements he made on their behalf was that we should not hold the wheat but that we should dispose of it at whatever price could be obtained. His next statement was that we were destroying cooperative effort. He said that Mr. McFarland was becoming a dictator in the west, that he had taken over the work of cooperative societies and that because of his activities cooperation was dying. I am sure the western farmers will be delighted indeed to have the hon. member from St. James street express their views in this chamber.
