However, I have before me some expressions from heads of cooperative institutions in western Canada, and in this connection I quote the observations of Mr. H. W. Wood, Chairman of the Alberta wheat pool:
I think the conference and so on have been a step in the right direction.
He was referring to the conferences from which the Ottawa agreements arose.
No one can tell the value of the acts or what might have resulted if all had been allowed to drift.
Then, I would like hon. members opposite to listen to this:
The government's stand when wheat was tobogganing toward the forty-cent a bushel mark almost two years ago was courageous, necessary and had vindicated itself.
Mr. Wood is anything but a politician. He never has been an exponent of Conservative principles nor has he been a partisan. Let us see what is said by the head of the Saskatchewan pool:

If the government goes out of the market, many farmers will go out of business"" declared Mr. Brouillette. Referring to Prime Minister R. B. Bennett's statement that federal stabilization operations had meant $25,000,000 to grain growers, the pool president thought the figure mentioned was very conservative.

I do not think that those gentlemen will thank the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth for attempting to express their views. The hon. member has said the government is destroying cooperative effort in western Canada. May I quote the magnificent effort made by the hon. member to promote cooperative effort in that particular part of Canada. Hon. members will recall that at the last session the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) introduced the Natural Products Marketing Act. I believe it is agreed by all people in western Canada that there never was a better conceived or a more far reaching piece of legislation placed before parliament. Never has there been any legislation so calculated to promote, assist and develop cooperative effort as was the marketing legislation introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. But what did the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth say about it? He delivered a most important address from his side of the chamber just before the vote was taken, in which he made the following observations:

I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that these three features, the autocratic and' compulsory feature of the marketing act itself, the tariff feature which does not belong to the bill, and the price spread feature without proper definitions, are all inimical to the welfare not only of the producers but of the people of Canada generally. And when I look at the act and realize

that the Prime Minister has completely failed to justify these vital and all-important features, which have been pointed out over and over again in this debate, I am reminded that whom the gods would destroy they first make mad. I say to my right hon. friend in all seriousness that if he passes this act and attempts to enforce it in the dominion he will find that his destruction will be certain and sure.

That was the magnificent attempt made by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth to promote cooperation in western Canada and to back up cooperative effort. ""Whom the gods would destroy they first make mad""-I wonder if the hon. member was referring to the gods of St. James street? I think perhaps he was. Let us see what the people of western Canada think about this terrible marketing act. I quote from the Western Producer, the paper that has the largest circulation among the producers and cooperatives of western Canada, and the organ of the cooperative societies in western Canada. In its issue of December 27, 1934, it says:

There are some people who oppose the Natural Products Marketing Act for the reason (a good and sufficient one in their eyes) that it was enacted by the federal government. They find it difficult to imagine anything good coming from the federal administration and even if it may look attractive on the surface, they feel sure there must be a catch in it somewhere.
We do not propose to argue with opponents of this kind because in such cases, reason is rarely of much effect.

That is the view taken by the cooperative organizations of western Canada with regard to the Natural Products Marketing Act. Now where does the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth get his inspiration? All through his speech he was quoting from the Financial Post, and again I thought I recognized the voice of St. James street. But surely the Financial Post does not speak for the cooperative organizations of western Canada, nor does it speak for the grain growers who have been helped by the holding up of the price of their grain.

Another very notable thing in the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth was that attempt that we have noticed in all the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite this session to condemn in the one breath and praise in the next the reform measures which the government has brought down. It simply means that hon. gentlemen opposite are seeking to evade responsibility outside the house for the criticisms which they level here at the legislation brought down by the government. In criticizing the work of Mr. John I. McFarland in supporting the wheat market the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth was very careful to leave a screen behind1 which
The Budget-Mr. Beynon
he could hide if he was charged with condemning the operations of Mr. McFarland; for at page 2116 of Hansard he said:
There has never been a word of criticism upon that score-

That is, about assisting the western farmer: -because everybody recognizes the importance of the western farmer as a producer, as a consumer and also as a citizen. What is the criticism? It is first from the point of view of the western farmer that the government instead of marketing the grain has virtually become his competitor.

In several places in the course of his address the hon. member was very careful to ring in that old, old statement that he was not finding any fault with Mr. McFarland or with the system. He just charged Mr. McFarland with trying to bring glory upon himself and upon this government through his operations, and the hon. gentleman intimated that Mr. McFarland was prepared to risk the credit of this country and1 the failure of his venture simply in order to bring glory on himself and on the government which my hon. friend says Mr. McFarland serves. Well, Mr. Speaker, if the western Liberals are prepared to go before the people of western Canada and fight the next election on the issue of the operations of Mr. John I. McFarland, or on the issue of the Natural Products Marketing Act brought in by the Minister of Agriculture we gladly accept that challenge here and now; but I venture to say that they are not prepared to stake their political fortunes on either one of those issues or on both of them'.

. The thought that comes to my mind first of all is to thank my constituents for the great honour which they did me in electing me as their representative for the historic riding of Selkirk. I have been heralded in the press during previous sessions as one of the radicals of the Conservative party. I am glad to-night that my party is the party of reform, and I am
(Mr. Beynon.J

pleased to announce to my constituents and this country to-night that I am proud to ibe a Conservative. I remember, Mr. Speaker, that it was a Liberal-Conservative party that presided at the birth of confederation under Sir John A. Macdonald. I remember also that it was under a great leader of this party, Sir Robert Borden, that this country took its place among the nations of the world in the day of Armageddon when Canada became a nation in fact as well as in name. I would remind my constituents and the country this evening that in the midst of the greatest depression in the history of this dominion, in the midst of trials and difficulties the like of which this country has never known this great party to which I say again I am proud to belong is, under the leadership of Sir Richard Bedford Bennett, the party of reform.

If any man ever deserved the title of ""Sir,"" if ever a knighthood might justly be conferred upon a Canadian for the services he has rendered, no one deserves it better than Richard Bedford Bennett.

Under his leadership Canada has struck its tents in the valley of depression and is now marching forward on the highway of reform. Under his able leadership, assisted by his able associates, such as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), whose budget we are now debating,-this country will yet reach a time and place when poverty will not work its awful havoc upon the Canadian people. Although perhaps it has been in the minds of many people in this country that it may have been hard for the hon. member for Selkirk to serve the Conservative party, I want to repeat that it is easy for him now because the Conservative party is the party of reform and progressive reconstruction.

I should like to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) in which he said that this was a policy of make believe and pretence. I admire the financial critic of the opposition, but as one soldier to another let me say to him that I think that statement was unworthy of a great soldier and a great Canadian. When one considers the difficulties which this country has been facing since 1930, when one realizes the efforts which this government has made to overcome the forces of depression which were world wide, I do not think anyone will agree with the hon. member when he says that our efforts at reform are make believe and pretence.
The Budget-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)

What is the position at the present time of the Liberal party? The Liberal party has now become the Tory party. I made this statement when I went home last year to my constituency. I said that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett) had changed shoes; they had reversed their roles. We find the Liberal party now upholding the constitution while the Conservative party is leading the way to reform. Once again the Conservative party is the party of the people, as it always has been, in spite of the criticism and camouflage of our Liberal opponents.

Let us look at these questions of unemployment and relief. To-day the Prime Minister is lying ill in the Chateau Laurier. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about the 1,250,000 Canadians who are on relief but I ask them: Who looked after those Canadians during the days of depression? Who warmed them against the winter's cold, who clothed them against the intemperate climate, who fed them in the face of starvation?

1060668,ca.proc.d.1935-04-01.20.5.20,1935-04-01,ed34bdbb-3fe8-4a8c-87a1-a2ad108b1e2b,ca.m.8281,Mr. STITT (Selkirk):,,SUPPLY-EUROPEAN SITUATION AMENDMENT BY MR. BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,I, 1935",,"I want to tell the

country a conversation I had with the Prime Minister. I wondered whether the provisions were constitutional, whether we were going to get into a lawsuit or not. I wondered whether there would be delay and whether every embarrassment possible would be placed in the way of the government's obtaining that gold from the banks. The Prime Minister said to me: ""It is just about time that this country found out who was running the country-the banks or the government."" If the Liberal party or the Labour party or the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation had passed legislation taking the gold from the banks and earmarking the profit on that gold for the Dominion of Canada, that fact would have been blazoned all over the country; it would have been looked upon as a most remarkable performance in the way of reform. One of the amazing points about the present situation is that the government has been almost afraid to advertise its virtues, almost reluctant to go out and tell the country just what these measures have meant in dollars and cents for the Canadian people.

Look at the work we have done for labour, and let the members of the Trades and Labour Congress pay attention to the remarks of their leader, Mr. Tom Moore, when he said: ""This budget is a poor man's budget."" We heard criticism the other day about t|he income tax rates. I wonder how many people in Canada know that if to-day a man has an income of 81,000,000, we take from him $527,000 in taxation. I wonder whether they realize that our rate of taxation on the higher incomes is greater than it is in Great Britain. Have we been given any praise for that?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,James Herbert Stitt,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ed34bdbb-3fe8-4a8c-87a1-a2ad108b1e2b&Language=E&Section=ALL

1060670,ca.proc.d.1935-04-01.20.5.22,1935-04-01,ed34bdbb-3fe8-4a8c-87a1-a2ad108b1e2b,ca.m.8281,Mr. STITT (Selkirk):,,SUPPLY-EUROPEAN SITUATION AMENDMENT BY MR. BOURASSA REAFFIRMING ADHESION TO TREATY FOR RENUNCIATION OF WAR,I, 1935",,"No more money! Well, we have found over $200,000,000 for unemployment relief; we have found money to guarantee the wheat pool operations, yes, and we have found money to guarantee the loans of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That matter is very easily explained to the people of Canada. I stated that this government was not afraid of public criticism; that it was not afraid of vested interests. Moreover it was not afraid to come to the assistance of a great corporation when it was necessary for the welfare of Canada that it should do so. What was the situation in connection with the $60,000,000 guarantee for the Canadian Pacific Railway? Its bonds were falling due in the

United States, and under the laws of that country it was impossible for that company to refloat loans in order to pay back its obligations. What would have happened had the government not come to the assistance of the Canadian Pacific Railway and enabled it to borrow money from the banks?-for let it be remembered that the Canadian Pacific has passed its dividends and has been losing money. The Canadian Pacific would have gone into the hands of a receiver; it would have gone into the possession of foreign investors. What would have happened to labour on the Canadian Pacific; what would have happened to the rates of pay; what would have happened to the business fabric of this country, had the government not had the courage, in spite of the political criticism that could be raised against such an action, to come to the aid of that great corporation, one that means almost the very life of the country?

Taxation of higher incomes! This budget has been described as a brave budget. The Minister of Finance must be complimented upon the manner of its presentation and the comprehensive review he has made of Canadian affairs. We have the policy of reform and the eight hour day, minimum wage and unemployment insurance measures. I told my constituents when I was elected that I would support an unemployment insurance bill. Whoever supposed that a Conservative government would enact a measure of unemployment insurance? If the Liberal party had enacted such a measure, the press of the country would have hailed it as a great work of reform, a great law of social justice. Surely it is about time that the people of Canada realize the services which this government has rendered to the nation.

Before the eleven o'clock adjournment, I ought to thank the Conservative party for the liberty they have given me, the freedom I have had within the party. I wonder how many members of the Liberal opposition have ever had the freedom that the member for Selkirk has had. Last year from my place I asked for reduction of interest rates, for the issuance of $100,000,000 of new money, for $50,000,000 worth of public works. What is the answer? We have had the policy of reform; we have had reduction of interest rates; we have had the issuance of new money to the extent of $50,000,000, and we have had an unemployment relief works policy aggregating $40,000,000.
On motion of Mr. Stitt (Selkirk) the debate was adjourned.
